statements.title: The Page We Were Never Given Time to Read
statements.snippet: A signature obtained by not giving you time to read the page isn't consent. Utahns are being asked to sign a page they were never shown — and we are asking Utah's delegation to separate what does not belong together.
statements.body:
A signature obtained by not giving you time to read the page isn't consent. We cannot fix that which we cannot see, and right now Utahns are being asked to sign a page they were never shown, whether they know it or not.

Every two years, Utahns walk into elementary schools and libraries and change their government without a single bullet fired. We treat that as ordinary because we have never had to live without it, but it is the rarest kind of power a free people can hold, and it only survives when the people can see, plainly, what they are agreeing to. That is the whole of the compact between Utahns and their government: we consent to be governed, and government earns that consent honestly, in the open, one decision at a time.

That compact was broken this week by how Congress made its decision, more than by the decision itself.

A voter eligibility measure, reshaping who can register to vote in this state, was merged by procedural maneuver into a sweeping defense authorization bill carrying major new commitments abroad. Two questions. Two very different sets of consequences. One vote. A lawmaker who supports election reform but has doubts about deepening foreign military entanglements has no way to say so. A lawmaker who supports the defense package but wants a harder look at citizenship requirements has no way to say that either. The bundling doesn't just obscure the decision from voters. It strips their own representatives of the ability to represent them.

We are not here to litigate either measure on its merits. Reasonable Utahns disagree, in good faith, about both. What we will not accept is a process built to make disagreement impossible to express. Utah voters deserve a line-item veto on matters this important — the ability to see two questions as two questions, and to hold their representatives accountable for two separate answers.

This is not a new problem, and it will not be the last time it's tried. It is precisely because it keeps working that it keeps happening. The fix is not complicated. Separate what does not belong together. Let each measure rise or fall on a vote that says what it means. Give the people the page, and give them time to read it.

We are asking Utah's delegation to do exactly that. We are asking every campaign, every civic organization, and every Utahn who has ever felt like their vote was a formality rather than a voice, to ask for the same thing, loudly and together.

The Utah Civic Compact is angry about this. You should be angry too.

A government that earns consent has nothing to fear from a clean vote. Only a process that depends on confusion needs to avoid one.
